title: The dark night
hookLine: John of the Cross: sometimes God feels absent, and that's part of the road

lines: A FRIAR IN A PRISON CELL.
cards: Some people of prayer describe a season like this, often only in a whisper. Prayer used to feel warm. Church used to move them.
God used to feel close. Then, sometimes for no clear reason, it goes quiet. The words feel empty.
Sitting down to pray is like talking into a closed room. They wonder if they're doing something wrong, or if it was all in their heads.
A Spanish friar, once locked in a tiny prison cell by men of his own religious order, came to write about that very experience. Today's word: dark night.

teach.b: John of the Cross was a Carmelite friar and a close colleague of Teresa, who you met yesterday. He worked with her to reform their order. Not everyone wanted reforming.
Early accounts say some of his own brothers seized him and locked him in a cell in Toledo so small and dark he had to stand on a stool to read by the light from a slit in the wall. He was beaten.
And in that darkness he composed poetry. After months, the story goes, he escaped at night by a rope of strips torn from blankets.

Around that time came a poem that begins: on a dark night. Later he wrote a book explaining it, The Dark Night. His idea: at the start, God often feels close and sweet, the way a mother carries a small child.

teach.h: GOD SETS THE CHILD DOWN TO WALK.
teach.b: But at some point, God sets the child down to walk. The warm feelings dry up. Prayer feels dark and empty.

John says this is not God leaving. It's God working in secret, loving you past your feelings, so that you come to love God for God, not for how God makes you feel. Bernard's four loves come back here.
John calls this darkness a guiding night, a night more kindly than the dawn. The Psalms said it long before: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee."

John distinguished this spiritual dryness from other kinds of suffering, and spiritual directors today add: if the darkness includes deep sadness or hopelessness, talk to someone, a doctor, a counselor, a trusted friend.

how: Christians in long dry seasons of prayer read John of the Cross, and spiritual directors use his idea of the dark night to help people keep praying when God feels far away.

o: a season when God feels far but still works
a night of prayer kept awake until dawn
a season of sin that drives God away

games.q: the dark night — tap the pairs.

s: John was imprisoned by men of his own order
some of his fellow friars locked him in a cell in Toledo.
John says the dark night means God has left
it's God working in secret, loving you past your feelings.
John treated every kind of suffering as the dark night
he distinguished spiritual dryness from other kinds of suffering.

games.q: prayer has gone dry. God feels absent. you wonder if you're doing it wrong. what does John of the Cross say is happening?
o: God is at work in secret, teaching you to walk.
God has given up on you.
games.why: the mother sets the child down so it can walk. the darkness is part of the road, not the end of it.

practice: Gently remember a time when God, or meaning, or hope, felt far away, and hold it at arm's length without reliving it; you got through it, or you're in it now. Say quietly: dark is not absent.
If you pray, you can simply sit in the dark with God, without needing to feel anything.

wordCard.voice: Dark night. John of the Cross's name for the season when God feels absent, and is still quietly at work.

orig.note: Spanish, in the Latin alphabet: dark night, the poem's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: dark is not absent. A flat season may be part of the road. Day two hundred seventy-seven, done.

sources.q: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee.

sources.ref: John of the Cross, The Dark Night, I.1; I.8–9; II.5
